To date, roughly 2,500 PPE items have been used, totaling about US$250,000, illustrating the resource burden on frontline care. WHO-installed three tents and 29 beds for maternity and pediatrics, plus oxygen concentrators, monitors, PPE, and medications, plus two ambulances dedicated to the Ebola response, expanded capacity. - US CDC will require all international air passengers bound for the United States to certify they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the prior 21 days, citing Ebola risk. article.articleHeadline: Avian influenza: Surveillance across Tamil Nadu.
article.articleSummary:
- Avian influenza surveillance across Tamil Nadu continues with the health department reporting no human cases to date. In Vandalur Zoological Park, several birds tested positive, prompting a two-day closure and ongoing precautionary measures. The department warns that avian influenza can spread to humans via infected birds and droppings, and notes that West Nile virus can be transmitted by mosquitoes from birds to people, increasing transmission risk. article.articleSummary:

They maintain ongoing TB education and urge residents to wear masks when coughing and to promptly seek screening at community health centers (puskesmas) or via health cadres if coughing. High-risk groups—including household and close contacts of TB patients, people with diabetes mellitus, smokers, the elderly, the malnourished, and people living with HIV—are advised to undergo chest radiography screening at puskesmas. The campaign promotes PHBS (Clean and Healthy Living Behaviors) and Germas (Healthy Living Community Movement) continuously. - 66 tuberculosis cases detected in Kepulauan Seribu (Thousand Islands), Jakarta, from January 1 to September 30, 2026, up from 55 cases in the same period of 2025. The Suku Dinas Kesehatan Kepulauan Seribu (Thousand Islands Health Office) attributes the rise to intensified surveillance and transmission interruption efforts. Authorities emphasize rapid treatment initiation to curb spread. Case finding has been expanded via Active Case Finding (ACF) campaigns and by improving the quality of Contact Investigations, complemented by lung screening using portable X-ray devices. Public health outreach continues to educate communities about tuberculosis transmission. No other diseases or locations are highlighted beyond Kepulauan Seribu. - Melioidosis (soil fever), caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, has infected 570 people and caused 45 deaths in four lower-northeastern provinces of Thailand through 22 October 2026: Buri Ram 245 cases/12 deaths; Surin 139/11; Nakhon Ratchasima 136/17; Chaiyaphum 50/5. The elderly (65+) are most affected, followed by those aged 55–64 and 45–54. Risk rises with prolonged rain and flooding as contact with wet soil and contaminated water increases. Transmission occurs via skin breaks, inhalation of contaminated dust or droplets, or ingestion. Farmers and people cleaning flood-affected areas are urged to take precautions. Protective measures include wearing rubber boots, gloves, long trousers or waterproof clothing; avoid contact with soil or water if wounds are open until healed.

article.articleHeadline: Chinese surveillance shows steep declines in reported vector-borne diseases
article.articleSummary: Five vector-borne diseases in China—typhus, dengue, leishmaniasis, malaria, and epidemic encephalitis B (EEB)—showed substantially lower reported incidence and deaths in 2020–2023 than 2013–2019. Overall incidence declined by 59.86% (95% CI -60.36% to -59.36%; P<0.001) and mortality by 83.72% (95% CI -87.86% to -78.18%; P<0.001). The analysis used province- and age-specific surveillance data for 2004–2020 from the Chinese CDC and national aggregate data for 2021–2023 from the National Health Commission; national trends extend through 2023. Malaria and EEB had the largest reductions; typhus and leishmaniasis were less affected. Southern provinces hosted most spatial hotspots in earlier periods. Methods included Joinpoint regression, STL seasonal-trend decomposition, interrupted time-series analysis, and SARIMA forecasts. The authors caution against attributing declines solely to COVID-19 measures, noting possible contributions from longer-term trends, control programs, and reporting changes, and call for reliable surveillance and adaptable forecasting.

article.articleHeadline: Clinical predictors of tracheobronchial tuberculosis and airway stenosis in
article.articleSummary: West China Hospital, southwestern China, conducted a retrospective single-centre study of 1,999 patients with confirmed pulmonary TB who underwent bronchoscopy between September 2013 and June 2019. Of these, 439 (22.0%) were diagnosed with tracheobronchial tuberculosis (TBTB), and among them 218 (49.7%) developed airway stenosis. Multivariable analysis identified three independent predictors of TBTB: female sex (odds ratio [OR] 5.726; 95% CI 1.913–17.133; p=0.002), age <50 years (OR 4.144; 95% CI 1.791–9.588; p=0.001), and positive sputum acid-fast smear (OR 2.494; 95% CI 0.998–6.636; p=0.050). However, CIs are wide and near 1 for the smear, reflecting uncertainty; associations describe relationships within the bronchoscopy-selected cohort rather than causality. Among TBTB patients, 218 (49.7%) developed airway stenosis. Timing and outcomes of stenosis were not detailed, and results cannot be extrapolated to unselected TB populations.

article.articleHeadline: External validation of a machine learning model for predicting liver injury in children with mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia
article.articleSummary: External validation of a machine learning-based tool to predict liver injury in pediatric mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia (MPP) patients. MPP is a leading cause of pediatric community-acquired pneumonia; liver injury occurs in about 10–30% of hospitalized children with MPP, worsening outcomes. The study used multicenter retrospective data from two Nanjing, China hospitals in 2023: development cohort at Nanjing Children's Hospital (n=885 training, 436 testing) and external validation at Nanjing Lishui People's Hospital (n=640). Liver injury was defined as ALT > 80 U/L. Ten algorithms were evaluated; the optimal model was chosen for discrimination and generalizability, using admission data within 24 hours (demographics, symptoms, imaging, and labs: CRP, WBC, LYMPH, NEUT, Hgb, PLT, LDH, CK, CK-MB, D-dimer, IL-6). An interactive web application was developed to support clinical use, with IRB approvals and waiver of consent noted.

article.articleHeadline: In France, the world's first case of human infection with the Shamonda virus has been recorded. The patient died.
article.articleSummary: France records the world's first human infection with Shamonda virus, with the patient dying in early October 2026. No broader public-health threat identified. The fatal case, in eastern France, follows a severe underlying illness that may have heightened susceptibility to infection; investigators are determining whether Shamonda contributed to death. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control is monitoring the situation and coordinating with French authorities and partners across Europe. Shamonda virus is transmitted by Culicoides midges and has previously been detected mainly in cattle, but also in horses, alpacas, sheep, and goats. There is no commercially available vaccine. The outbreak also concerns livestock, with nine French dairy farms reporting milk production declines of up to 75% in infected herds. A separate report notes a Chinese study describing a new tick-borne virus ALTNV.

article.articleHeadline: Blood samples showed longer chikungunya detection in hospitalized patients
article.articleSummary: Chikungunya virus dynamics and persistence were evaluated in 53 hospitalized patients in Nanning, Guangxi Province, China, during the 2025 outbreak—the largest recorded in the country. Across 506 specimens, serum positivity was 81.20%, plasma 72.50%, saliva 11.03%, and urine 4.73%. Ct values were lower in serum/plasma than saliva/urine in the first four days, indicating stronger blood-based detection during acute illness. Generalized estimating equations showed saliva positivity dropping from 52.2% on day 1 to 0.7% by day 7; blood positivity declined more gradually, with serum and plasma above ~85% on day 3 and about 30% by day 7. Median detection durations were 5.8 days in serum and plasma (CI 4.8–6.9 and 4.7–7.1), and 3.5 days in saliva (CI 3.0–4.1); urine data were too sparse for a median estimate. Limitations: hospitalized, single city, not measuring infectious virus, not generalizable to mild cases.

article.articleHeadline: Revisiting the CDC's Original Mission, Promoting Tuberculosis Knowledge — Yongzhou City Center for Disease Control and Prevention Launches a Photography Touring Exhibition "Seeing Health in Disease Control"
article.articleSummary: On 2026-10-22, Yongzhou City Center for Disease Control and Prevention hosted a tuberculosis-focused photography touring exhibit as part of a province-wide campaign, Seeing Health in Disease Control, organized by the Hunan Provincial CDC. The site showcased disease-control work through photographs at the center entrance, inviting staff and residents to view, discuss, and reaffirm the CDC’s mission. Yongzhou CDC will continue to leverage science communication resources to strengthen internal capacity and broaden TB prevention messaging citywide, safeguarding public health.

The region’s viruses can originate from China and Nepal, and influenza or a common cold could occur, though none are typical for high altitude. She concludes the reported symptoms most closely resemble hypoxia — oxygen deprivation from reduced air pressure and oxygen at extreme altitude, exacerbated by exertion. No laboratory confirmation, infection source, or ongoing outbreak is reported, and the case is described as unknown disease on Everest with no indications of imported/exported cases.

article.articleHeadline: Phase II Clinical Trial of SYH2066 for the Treatment of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection Officially Initiated in China
article.articleSummary: RSV infection: Phase II trial of SYH2066 officially initiated in China, with the first clinical site in the country. SYH2066 is a small-molecule RSV fusion protein (F protein) inhibitor, classified as a Class 1 chemical drug, which binds to the RSV F protein to prevent its conformational change and membrane fusion, blocking viral entry and replication. China’s National Medical Products Administration approved the clinical trial in September 2025. A preceding Phase I study in healthy Chinese participants demonstrated favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profiles for oral administration. The current Phase II is multi-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, evaluating efficacy and safety in Chinese adults with RSV infection; recruitment and screening are actively underway.

article.articleHeadline: Has the plague crossed the mysterious 0.63 threshold? From a Siberian case to the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, global warming reveals a new battleground for epidemics.
article.articleSummary: Death of a 28-year-old female researcher at Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute (Siberia) in early October raises questions about a plague exposure in Irkutsk, Russia; media reports of a second death are not supported by WHO data, and about 200 contacts completed latent-period monitoring by Oct 9 with no secondary transmission; final pathology results are pending. The event underscores Eurasian plague concerns amid climate change. A multinational 18-year Scientific Reports study finds warming’s effect on plague is not universal but depends on ecological thresholds, notably ground squirrel density. In Mongolia and northern China’s low- to mid-altitude grasslands, warming promotes flea reproduction and plague transmission if ground squirrel density exceeds 0.63 per hectare. In the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau at elevations above 4000 m, high UV and aridity suppress fleas and pathogen activity. Public health guidance emphasizes avoiding contact with wild rodents, protective clothing, DEET, veterinary flea control, and prompt medical care with travel history.

article.articleHeadline: Brain-Eating Amoeba: How It Enters Through the Nose and Why It Can Be Fatal.
article.articleSummary: Catamarca, Argentina, reports the death of a 10-year-old boy from primary amebic meningoencephalitis caused by Naegleria fowleri, a free-living amoeba in warm fresh waters. Transmission occurs when water enters the nasal passages during head immersion. Incubation ranges from 1 day to 2 weeks; symptoms progress rapidly to fever, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, confusion, and coma. PAM is nearly always fatal, with mortality near 100% and death commonly within 72 hours of onset. Identified in Australia, a pool outbreak occurred in Europe. In Latin America, cases have been reported in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Venezuela; the US documented its first case in 1988. Esteros del Iberá, Corrientes, and coastal zones are high-risk, with water temperatures up to 40–45 C. Prevention relies on rapid diagnosis and treatment; options include amphotericin B, fluconazole, azithromycin, and rifampin. No proven environmental control exists; use nasal clips and minimize splashes, and alert clinicians.

article.articleHeadline: Cholera: A Disease That Has Killed Thousands Can Be Treated With Water, Salts, and Sugar in the Correct Proportion.
article.articleSummary: Cholera, an intestinal infection caused by Vibrio cholerae, can cause rapid, severe dehydration and death if untreated. Most patients recover with prompt rehydration using oral rehydration solution; severe cases require intravenous fluids in hospital. Transmission occurs mainly through water or foods contaminated with the bacteria, especially where drinking water is unsafe and sewage treatment is inadequate. Symptoms include profuse, watery diarrhea (rice-water stools) and vomiting, with dehydration signs such as intense thirst, dry mouth, sunken eyes, reduced urination, cramps, weakness, rapid pulse, and low blood pressure. Some infections are asymptomatic yet shed bacteria, sustaining transmission. John Snow linked 1854 London outbreaks to a contaminated public water pump. In Brazil, cholera re-emerged in the early 1990s, highlighting water, sanitation, and hygiene challenges. Prevention emphasizes safe water (treated/boiled), handwashing, washing produce with safe water, keeping water storage clean, and, where appropriate, oral cholera vaccines during outbreaks, though vaccines do not replace sanitation.

Health organizations warn that unclear information hinders risk assessment, yet classify the immediate risk as low; health systems should guide clinicians and monitor exposed individuals. Pneumonic plague is the most severe Yersinia pestis infection and can present as bubonic, septicemic, or pneumonic forms; without prompt treatment, pneumonic plague has high mortality. It incubates in one to two days and transmits via respiratory droplets or aerosols; infection can also result from laboratory exposure. Pneumonia can be secondary to a bubonic infection from fleas, not directly respiratory. In Brazil, plague was introduced in Santos in late 19th century, with outbreaks in port cities including Rio de Janeiro; the last human case was 2005. Ceará and Teresópolis were foci, with rodent reservoirs sustaining vigilance.

Incomplete therapy—often penicillin given in three doses seven days apart—raises reinfection and transmission risks; partner treatment and condom use are advised.

Symptoms include redness, swelling, pain and warmth on the face; fever, chills and malaise may occur in advanced cases. If the infection reaches the danger triangle (corners of the mouth to the nasal bridge and around the eyes), there is a higher risk of intracranial spread, potentially causing cavernous sinus thrombosis or meningitis. Causes include squeezing pimples, poor skin hygiene, and immune compromise (diabetes, HIV, corticosteroid use). Prevention emphasizes not popping pimples, keeping skin clean, using appropriate products, and dermatologic management of acne. Seek medical care promptly if signs appear to prevent complications.

article.articleHeadline: Modus Therapeutics: SEVUSMART study of sevuparin in children with severe malaria published in Nature Communications
article.articleSummary: SEVUSMART, a Phase Ib study of sevuparin as adjunctive therapy for severe malaria in children, enrolled 23 patients in Kenya and Zambia and identified a maximum tolerated dose of 3 mg/kg per infusion. article.articleHeadline: A mother and her child both have influenza A.
article.articleSummary: As of 22 October 2026, two influenza A cases were reported in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam: a mother and her 7-year-old son, Huy. The mother first developed runny nose, sore eyes, and mild fever with chills; two days later Huy showed similar symptoms. Rapid tests confirmed influenza A in both. They received antiviral therapy, fever management, fluids, and nutritional support, isolated in separate rooms to reduce transmission. After five days, both improved. Dr. Dat notes influenza A has a 1–4 day incubation (average 2) and remains contagious one day before symptoms and early in the illness. Transmission is mainly via respiratory droplets, with crowded, enclosed spaces increasing risk. Common symptoms include abrupt fever, cough, sore throat, headache, and muscle aches; some cases are milder. Complications can include pneumonia or dehydration. Prevention includes masks, hand hygiene, ventilation, and not sharing utensils. The family was unvaccinated but plans influenza vaccination after recovery.

article.articleHeadline: Why can Influenza A cause complications?
article.articleSummary: Influenza A complications arise when the virus directly injures lung tissue or when bacterial superinfection or preexisting conditions worsen disease. In Vietnam, influenza A commonly presents with fever, cough, sore throat, headache, myalgia and fatigue, with most patients recovering in about a week, but it can descend to the lower respiratory tract to cause viral pneumonia. Lung injury damages epithelial cells and triggers inflammation, impairing gas exchange and causing rapid breathing and hypoxemia; severe cases may progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), requiring high-flow oxygen, noninvasive ventilation or intubation. Bacterial superinfection—especially Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus—can follow flu, with fever returning, worsened cough, chest pain or dyspnea, and potential sepsis. Antibiotics should not be used routinely. At-risk groups include those over 65, pregnancy, chronic heart/lung disease, diabetes, kidney disease, neurological or immunodeficiency conditions; asthma and COPD can worsen. Vaccination reduces risk, per clinicians at Tam Anh General Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

article.articleHeadline: The Director and the Female Student Receive HIV Test Results After the Visit to Saigon on October 20
article.articleSummary: On October 20 in Ho Chi Minh City, a director based in Hanoi and a female student living there were diagnosed HIV positive after visiting HIV tests via Huỳnh Sachi, a health worker. Public health expert Dr. Nguyen Tan Thu advised: consistent condom use for vaginal or anal sex, HIV/STI testing when at risk, PrEP for those at risk, PEP after exposure, avoid needle sharing, HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, and prompt medical care for symptoms. article.articleHeadline: Drug-resistant Salmonella found in Metro Manila chicken meat -- study
article.articleSummary: Salmonella spp. isolated from retail broiler chicken meat in Metro Manila show high antibiotic resistance, per a DOST-FNRI study. Researchers warn that antimicrobial resistance complicates treatment of Salmonella infections, reflecting broader foodborne disease concerns. Philippine Salmonella infections increased by 42% to 13,000 in 2023. Chicken remains an important protein source, but safe handling is essential. The study sampled Salmonella from retail wet markets and supermarkets across Metro Manila, emphasizing prevention through proper cooking, avoidance of cross-contamination, thorough handwashing, separate utensils, and refrigeration.

article.articleHeadline: Polio Still Exists - No Child Is Safe Until Every Child Is Safe
article.articleSummary: World Polio Day on October 24 highlights the ongoing effort to eradicate poliomyelitis, a highly contagious viral infection causing paralysis and death. Rotary International began its polio campaign on September 29, 1979, in Makati, Philippines, when the first vaccine drops were given; the initial effort immunized about 6 million children at a cost of $7,60,000. Polio Plus launched in 1985, and Rotary became a founder member of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative in 1988 with WHO, UNICEF and CDC. Rotary has contributed over $2.1 billion and countless volunteer hours to protect 3 billion children in 122 countries; Gates Foundation funds are matched 2:1. Today only Afghanistan and Pakistan remain polio-endemic, with cases reduced by 99.9%. India was polio-free in 2014, but AFP and wastewater surveillance continue, aided by National Immunization Days, vaccinating in conflict zones.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue and El Niño: How Spring Temperatures Can Forecast the Risk in Argentina.
article.articleSummary: Argentina's dengue risk linked to El Niño and spring warmth: A 17-year study (2009–2025) across 473 northern/central departments analyzed 817,699 dengue cases. Dengue outbreaks in Argentina peak November–May. Findings show El Niño years markedly increase dengue risk, independent of seasonal climate; spring temperatures relate to summer transmission in a non-linear way. Higher summer temperatures and humidity amplify risk, and populations near landfills face greater exposure. The work, a Research Square preprint under formal review by the International Journal of Health Geographics, identifies where and when higher risk occurs (including the 2024 epidemic) but struggles to quantify outbreak size. For 2026–2027, regional climate forecasts vary: center and Litoral expect rainfall above normal, while Cuyo/Córdoba/western Santa Fe/La Pampa may be cooler; other regions show normal-to-warm patterns. This supports region-specific dengue prevention planning.

article.articleHeadline: Taste of Life: How plague controls disrupted domestic life in colonial Pune
article.articleSummary: Bubonic plague struck Bombay in August 1896; Poona (Pune) surveillance began at the Poona railway station on September 30, 1896, with first local cases recorded in December 1896. After the Epidemic Diseases Act (Act III of 1897) gained assent February 4, 1897, Walter Charles Rand was appointed chair of the Poona Plague Committee (March 9, 1897), with systematic operations starting March 13, 1897. Interventions included house-to-house inspections, removal of suspected patients to hospitals or segregation facilities, disinfection, and movement restrictions, amid distrust over intrusions into domestic, religious, and caste practices. Official records appear in municipal/provincial publications; no central public kitchen existed, as cooking and food supply were handled within segregation camps and hospitals. The General Segregation Camp on Shankarshet Road was the main confinement site, with smaller camps at Wanowrie and Kondhwa. Food policies varied: before compulsory detention, one free meal per day; during detention, two annas daily for labouring classes (others usually none). Evictions disrupted households; military searches raised privacy and caste/religion concerns. Criticism appeared in Mahratta and Kesari; petitions to the Bombay Legislative Council (Aug 5, 1897). Violence followed: Chapekar brothers attacked Government House on June 22, 1897.

article.articleSummary: As of 2026-10-22, Odisha, India: in adults with grade III/IV unilateral/bilateral lower-limb lymphedema due to lymphatic filariasis, an exploratory open-label trial (12 months) of individualized homoeopathic treatment enrolled 104 participants; 61 dropped out, 43 completed all monthly follow-ups. Laboratory and objective measures showed concurrent signal of improvement, but absence of numerical effect sizes and the open-label design limit causal inference. The authors frame results as exploratory signals needing confirmation in larger controlled studies; lymphatic filariasis morbidity remains a public-health challenge with mass drug administration addressing transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Two novel Silviavirus phages with lytic activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: genomic and phenotypic characterization
article.articleSummary: Two novel Silviavirus bacteriophages, CARØ0038 and CARØ0046, isolated from sewage in Davangere, Karnataka, India, lyse methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Transmission electron microscopy shows icosahedral heads with short tails typical of Caudoviricetes. Genome sizes are 120,939 bp and 136,667 bp, encoding 227 and 225 predicted proteins with GC contents of 29.5% and 29.1%, respectively; phylogenomics place them in genus Silviavirus with unclear species-level assignment. Both phages exhibit efficient lytic activity against MRSA at an multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1, with latent periods of 15–20 minutes and burst sizes of 49 and 47 PFU per cell. Infectivity remains high up to 37 °C, declines at 45–50 °C, and is undetectable at 60 °C. Maximum recovery occurs at pH 7 (tested within 6–8). Host range includes all 28 tested MRSA isolates and methicillin-susceptible S. aureus; no lysis of S. epidermidis or S. saprophyticus under tested conditions. No known antimicrobial resistance or virulence genes identified. These findings support further exploration of CARØ0038 and CARØ0046 as phage-based antimicrobials against S. aureus, including MRSA.

article.articleHeadline: Epidemiological surveillance of respiratory infections: detecting outbreaks before they spread
article.articleSummary: Epidemiological surveillance translates laboratory results into public health alerts to detect outbreaks of respiratory infections early, linking isolated cases by area and time. The WHO aims by 2030 for 24-hour detection of emerging threats. Surveillance analyzes circulating pathogens, prevalence trends, affected populations, and transmission links; it guides interventions such as chemoprophylaxis, targeted vaccination, isolation and risk communication, and evaluates intervention impact. Classifications include sporadic, endemic, seasonal, cluster and outbreak. Illustrative cases: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) shows vaccination reduces invasive disease, yet the EU/EEA reported 5,234 confirmed Hib invasive cases in 2023; a Hamburg, Germany Hib outbreak (Sept 2024–Aug 2025) among middle-aged drug users and homeless people prompted an update to vaccination guidelines. Bordetella pertussis vs B. holmesii matters for diagnosis; 2024 EU/EEA recorded 209,674 pertussis cases (54.9/100k), mainly infants <1 and ages 10–14. Northern India (2019–2023) shows notable B. holmesii circulation, including unvaccinated patients with negative pertussis IgG.

article.articleHeadline: Could nutritional supplements protect the family from the threat of TB?

Outcomes focus on bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and extrapulmonary TB among household contacts. The study builds on Indian Lancet findings showing up to a 48% reduction in pulmonary TB risk with nutritional support, aiming to inform national and global TB prevention policy. article.articleHeadline: Gorontalo Provincial Government strengthens the role of the TNI Hospital in TB control.
article.articleSummary: Gorontalo province strengthens the role of the TNI Hospital (RS Tk IV dr Eddy Kounang Gorontalo) in TB control, with emphasis on drug-resistant TB (TB-DR). The Dinas Kesehatan, Pengendalian Penduduk dan Keluarga Berencana (Dinkes P2KB) notes ongoing on-the-job training for TB drug-resistant management at the hospital, as part of expanding health-service networks to improve TB detection, diagnosis, and treatment access. TB control is framed as a shared responsibility requiring multi-sector engagement, in line with Presidential Regulation No. 67/2021 on TB elimination, including collaboration with TNI and Polri. The province seeks MoH support for Mobile X-Ray facilities to bolster services at RS Tk IV dr Eddy Kounang Gorontalo. The hospital already conducts health screenings, such as Free Health Checks (CKG) and TB screening, signaling active implementation of screening and referral strengthening within Gorontalo, including Gorontalo Regency.

article.articleHeadline: [NNA] Myanmar's healthcare system collapse, concerns about the regional spread of infectious diseases | Aju Economy
article.articleSummary: Myanmar's civil war has collapsed its healthcare system, shrinking medical professionals per 10,000 people from about 18 to 3, fueling outbreaks of cholera, malaria, and tuberculosis. The collapse is compounded by displacement, physician migration abroad, and targeted destruction of hospitals and clinics. A 2025 earthquake killed about 5,000 and damaged 600+ health facilities; a year later roughly 300,000 still lack access to care. Think Global Health warns this could become a long-term regional public health crisis absent international support. Cholera remains active since 2024–2026, with WHO warning of possible spread to India. Malaria cases have tripled since the widening conflict, with up to 70% of the population at risk. Drug-resistant malaria parasites are dominant in parts of Myanmar and are spreading to India and Thailand; non-drug-resistant strains are entering Bangladesh. In Thailand, 2023 malaria cases reached 16,675, with over 40% imported, chiefly from Myanmar. Urgent cross-border public health measures needed.

article.articleHeadline: Scoping review maps antimalarial resistance markers across Southeast Asia
article.articleSummary: Scoping review of 25 studies on Plasmodium vivax antimalarial resistance across Southeast Asia, including Cambodia, Lao PDR, Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand and the Philippines, found antifolate resistance markers widespread, with two multilocus haplotypes pvdhfr F57I/L+S58R+T61M+S117N/T and pvdhps A383G+A553G linked to reduced drug susceptibility and, in some populations, slower parasite clearance and higher sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine treatment failure. Chloroquine resistance signals (pvcrt-o K10 insertion; pvmdr1 polymorphisms—T958M, Y976F, F1076L) were frequently reported but showed inconsistent associations with phenotypic susceptibility or clinical outcomes, so they should not be treated as uniform predictors. pvK12 mutations were uncommon; no validated molecular marker for artemisinin resistance in P. vivax. Data on resistance to ACT partner drugs were sparse and heterogeneous. Evidence is sparse, geographically uneven, and based on 25 studies; molecular detection alone cannot reliably establish clinical significance. Authors call for integrated molecular, phenotypic, and therapeutic surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Dr. Altshtein commented on a case of Shamonda virus detection in a human.
article.articleSummary: France reports the first laboratory-confirmed human case of Shamonda virus infection, with one patient diagnosed. Virologist Anatoly Altshtein, chief scientist at Gamaleya National Research Center, notes that this solitary infection does not herald an epidemic and human cases remain exceptional. Shamonda virus, identified in the mid-1960s, previously affected only livestock. In humans, it is described as causing relatively mild illness with fever, fatigue, and diarrhea, while animals generally recover. In Russia, researchers report an imported case of melioidosis in a woman returning from Thailand. Exposure likely occurred on a farm with elephants during travel, and the patient was hospitalized in severe condition. The article discusses whether melioidosis could spark an outbreak in Russia, but provides no evidence of wider transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Global project targets African swine fever prediction, prevention
article.articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) prediction and prevention project ASF Nexus aims to improve outbreak forecasting and control, with a focus on the UK and Southeast Asia. Led by Pete Dodd, professor of mathematical modelling and epidemiology at the University of Sheffield, the international program brings together bioscience, mathematics, economics and behavioral science to understand ASF spread and prevention. Research starts in Sarawak, Malaysian Borneo, with potential regional expansion, and examines how farming practices, economic pressures and governance influence transmission. By combining biological studies with economic and social analysis, ASF Nexus will model outbreaks, assess intervention costs, and develop open-access predictive tools and locally relevant guidance for farming communities and policymakers. The £54 million UKRI investment backs 18 projects addressing biological threats; collaborators include Liverpool's Pandemic Institute, Liverpool John Moores University, Sarawak Infectious Disease Centre, and Thailand's NCGEB.
